title: Literature — Chairil, Pram and the pantun
goal: Talk about a novel and a poem in Indonesian, using the vocabulary of literary discussion, read the old spelling of classic texts, and write your own *pantun* — the four-line verse form Indonesians still use at weddings, in speeches and in jokes.
bekal: discuss a book: *tokoh utama, latar, alur, tema, amanat*, and react with *kagum sekaligus kesal*
read pre-1972 spelling: *djalang → jalang, tjinta → cinta, oentoek → untuk*
write a *pantun* with a *sampiran*, an *isi* and an a-b-a-b rhyme

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Diskusi buku di TIM
dialogs.intro: Early June. Dr. Lestari, now teaching in Jakarta, has lent Sarah her copy of *Bumi Manusia*. They meet at the H.B. Jassin literary documentation centre in Taman Ismail Marzuki (TIM), Cikini, to talk about it.

notes: **Bumi Manusia (1980).** The first volume of Pramoedya Ananta Toer's *Tetralogi Buru*, set around 1898 in colonial Surabaya. Minke, a young Javanese aristocrat at a Dutch elite school, falls in love and runs into the limits of colonial law. It is available in English as *This Earth of Mankind*, and reading the two side by side is excellent B2 practice.

**Pribumi.** Literally "children of the soil", the colonial legal category for indigenous Indonesians, ranked below Europeans and "foreign Orientals". Pram uses it deliberately. ⚠️ Today the word is politically charged, and a 1998 presidential instruction told government bodies to stop using *pribumi* and *non-pribumi*; use it only when discussing history.

**Pulau Buru, tahanan politik.** After 1965, thousands of alleged leftists were held without trial; Pram spent 1969–1979 on Buru, in eastern Indonesia. Denied paper at first, he told his stories to fellow prisoners (*sesama tahanan*). *Tahanan politik* is shortened to *tapol*. *Secara lisan* means "orally"; its written counterpart is *secara tertulis*.

**Kagum sekaligus kesal.** *Sekaligus* — "at the same time, in one go" — lets you hold two reactions at once, which is what good literature does to you. It also works for actions: *sekaligus makan siang* ("and have lunch while we're at it").

**Binatang jalang.** In Chairil's poem *jalang* means "wild, untamed", the first meaning in KBBI. ⚠️ In modern speech *jalang* is mostly an insult for a promiscuous woman, so quote Chairil freely but don't describe anyone as *jalang*. The poem was first published under the title *Semangat* (Spirit).

**Menendang.** "To kick" — used figuratively, as in English "punchy". Chairil (1922–1949) is the leading poet of the *Angkatan '45* (the Generation of '45), and he broke with the flowery Malay of earlier poets. His lines are quoted on T-shirts, murals and protest banners to this day.

grammars.title: Talking about a book
body: Indonesian schools teach literary analysis with a fixed set of terms. Use them and a teacher, a bookseller or an exam marker will know exactly what you mean.
after: *Kilas balik* is "flashback", and *gaya bahasa* is "style" or "figure of speech". *Amanat* is a very Indonesian category: school readers are expected to find the lesson a story teaches, and a review that ignores it can feel unfinished.

grammars.title: Old spelling you will meet
body: Chairil wrote *binatang djalang*, and texts from before 1972 look strange until you know six letter swaps. Read the left-hand column aloud with the right-hand spelling and it becomes ordinary Indonesian.
after: ⚠️ The *j → y* swap is the tricky one: in old texts *saja* can mean *saya* (I), and *jang* is *yang*. The history of these reforms, and why *oe* went first, is part of Unit 10.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Pantun untuk Kinan
dialogs.intro: Mid-June. Rina and Andi's daughter Kinan was born ten days ago. Sarah visits them at home in Tebet with a present: a pantun, handwritten on good paper.

notes: **The pantun.** Four lines, eight to twelve syllables each, rhyming a-b-a-b. Lines 1–2 are the *sampiran*, an image that sets up the sound; lines 3–4 are the *isi*, the actual message. The pantun is oral Malay poetry centuries old, and in 2020 UNESCO inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage, nominated jointly by Indonesia and Malaysia.

**Gendong.** To carry a child in your arms, on your hip or in a sling (*kain gendongan*). *Mau gendong?* is the classic offer to a visitor. Other baby vocabulary for Unit 15: *menyusui* (to breastfeed), *begadang* (to stay up all night), *popok* (nappy).
**Terharu.** "Moved, touched" — the feeling that brings tears of the good kind. It is one of the feelings Unit 15 will pin down precisely. *Aduh* here is not pain but emotion overflowing.

**Jakarta banget.** *Banget* after a noun turns it into an adjective: *Jakarta banget* (so Jakarta), *Sarah banget* (so typically Sarah). Tanah Abang is the huge textile market in central Jakarta, so buying cloth there is a perfectly Jakartan image.

**Tante Sarah.** Children call women of their parents' generation *Tante* (from Dutch) and men *Om*. In Javanese families you may hear *Bulik* and *Paklik* for aunt and uncle. From today, Sarah is *Tante Sarah* to Kinan for life.

**Garing, bacain.** *Garing* is "crispy, dry" — and in slang, a joke that falls flat, much as English speakers call a joke "dry" or "lame". Unit 14 is all about humour. *Bacain* is Jakarta *-in* for *bacakan* (read it aloud for someone).

grammars.title: Writing your own pantun
body: Poets start with the message and build the *sampiran* backwards. Here is how Sarah wrote hers.

head: Step
What to do
Sarah's pantun
rows: lines 3 and 4: what you want to say
*Kinan sayang, tidurlah tenang, / semoga tumbuh sehat dan kuat.*
the last sound of lines 3 and 4
an everyday image with the same endings
the rhythm should swing in two halves

after: Kinds of pantun you will meet: *pantun nasihat* (advice), *pantun jenaka* (funny), *pantun cinta* (love, often cheesy), *pantun teka-teki* (riddles) and *pantun anak-anak* (children's). Politicians and MCs love opening or closing with a pantun, and the audience is expected to reply *Cakep!* ("Nice one!") after the second line.

blocks.text: You don't need to read them all, but knowing these names will let you follow any conversation about Indonesian books. Most are available in English translation, which makes them ideal for parallel reading.

blocks.text: For a first Indonesian novel, *Laskar Pelangi* is the gentlest: short chapters, school vocabulary and a well-known film adaptation to watch afterwards. Save Pram for when a long sentence no longer frightens you.

Useful phrases for a book club: *Menurut saya, bagian terkuatnya adalah…* (for me the strongest part is…), *Saya kurang suka akhir ceritanya* (I didn't much like the ending), *Tokoh ini bikin saya gregetan* (this character drove me up the wall), and the essential *Jangan spoiler, ya!*
A handful of classic pantun are known by everyone and quoted at farewells, in speeches and in class. Learn one or two; they buy enormous goodwill.
